items.question: A web search endpoint received a request whose message parameter contained a quote followed by an always-true comparison, and it still answered with HTTP 200 and a larger response body than ordinary searches. What describes a database query being assembled unsafely from request input?

Repeated requests to one parameter differed only by true-or-false conditions appended to the value. The application showed no error text, but response sizes and timing changed according to the condition, as if the database were answering yes-or-no questions.
File download requests carried repeated parent-directory sequences in the filename parameter, and the server returned a file that is not inside the intended download folder.
The filename parameter was percent-encoded so that it climbed out of the current directory with dot-dot-slash style steps, aiming at system configuration files rather than the files the page serves.

An image-import feature accepted a web address from the user, and the server then made an outbound request to a private internal address and to the cloud instance metadata address, returning the fetched content to the requester.
A parameter value contained a semicolon followed by a shell command, and the web server's process started a child process whose arguments matched that text.
Text supplied by a user in a template field was evaluated by the application's scripting engine, and the server then ran statements written by the requester inside its own runtime.
An administrative function responded successfully to requests that carried no session cookie and no credentials at all.
A signed-in ordinary user retrieved another user's records by changing an identifier in the address, and the server never checked whether that user was permitted to see them.
A parameter containing an HTML script element was echoed without escaping inside the response page, so it would run in the browser of anyone who opened the crafted link.
Request parameter values were altered and extra parameters were appended so that the backend processed the request differently from what the page intended.
Malformed, oversized and special-character values were accepted by many endpoints without any check of their form, length or allowed characters.
Investigate a suspected SQL injection against the search endpoint: the request contained an OR 1 equals 1 style condition.
Blind SQL injection is suspected because response timing differs between boolean conditions injected into one parameter.
The SQL injection appears to have reached the operating system, because commands ran on the database host through a database feature.
Path traversal attempt: download requests used dot-dot-slash sequences to reach files outside the web root.
Server-side request forgery is suspected: the application fetched a URL chosen by the requester and returned the response.
OS command injection in a network diagnostics form: the submitted host value included shell metacharacters.
Generic command injection: a command string built from request parameters was executed, and the interpreter involved is not yet known.
Authentication bypass: a protected page loaded without a valid login after the request was altered.
Reflected cross-site scripting in the search results page: the query value appeared unescaped in the HTML.
Special characters were passed unneutralized to some downstream interpreter, and the kind of interpreter is not yet known: a general injection weakness.

Before injecting anything, the intruder first inventoried the application's links with a web crawler and captured network traffic to find which inputs feed database queries. What describes that opening exploration step?
